study.title: Acts 13 - The mission to the Gentiles and the answer to the word of God
study.overview: Acts 13 shows the church of Antioch discerning, in prayer and fasting, the sending of Barnabas and Saul by the Holy Spirit. The narrative advances from the opposition of a false prophet in Cyprus to Paul's sermon in Antioch of Pisidia, in which he recalls the story of Israel to show that Jesus is the fulfillment of the promise made to his parents. The chapter highlights that salvation is first announced to the Jews, but also to the Gentiles, and ends with a double response: rejection and persecution of some, joy and fullness of the Spirit among the disciples.

outline.title: Sending Barnabas and Saul and confrontation in Cyprus
outline.explanation: The church in Antioch serves the Lord with fasting and prayer, and the Holy Spirit separates Barnabas and Saul into a specific work. In Cyprus, the proclamation of the word finds resistance in Barjesus, but the proconsul Sergius Paul believes in seeing the divine judgment on the opponent and listening to the teaching of the Lord.

outline.title: Arrival at Pisidia and the beginning of Paul's sermon
outline.explanation: After the passage through Perge, John separates from them and returns to Jerusalem. In Antioch of Pisídia, Paul is invited to speak in the synagogue and begin his message by remembering the choice of Israel, the exodus, the desert, the judges, Saul and David, to prepare the connection between the history of Israel and the arrival of Jesus.

outline.title: Jesus, dead and risen, as a proclamation of forgiveness and justification
outline.explanation: Paul declares that the word of salvation is sent to the children of Abraham and to those who fear God. He claims that the leaders of Jerusalem fulfilled the Scriptures in condemning Jesus, but that God raised him up. Then apply the Scriptures to show that in Jesus there is forgiveness and justification for everyone who believes, something that the law of Moses could not fully grant.

outline.title: Rejection of some Jews, host of the Gentiles and final joy
outline.explanation: Many Gentiles ask to hear again, and a crowd meets the following Saturday. Envy leads some Jews to contradict Paul, which makes the apostles turn more directly to the Gentiles, according to the vocation of being light to the nations. The word spreads, persecution arises, the missionaries are expelled, but the disciples remain full of joy and the Holy Spirit.

study.context: The chapter takes place in the context of the church's expansion beyond Jerusalem and shows Antioch as a missionary sending point. The text mentions Jewish synagogues in different cities, which explains why Paul's preaching begins between God-fearing Jews and Gentiles. The notes received highlight that Barnabas and Saul were separated with prayer and fasting, that the journey to the island of Cyprus included preaching in the synagogues, and that the speech in Antioch of Pisídia serves to Scripturally justify the mission to the Gentiles and the attitude of the apostles to rejection.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that the Christian mission is born from the direction of the Holy Spirit, not just human planning. The laying on of hands in prayer recognizes the call of God, but does not create it. It is also seen that the gospel confronts spiritual and human opposition: in Cyprus, the resistance of a false prophetic mage contrasts with the faith of the proconsul. In Paul's sermon, the history of Israel is read as a preparation for Christ: the God of promise acts in liberation, in the preservation of the people, in the kingdom of David, and finally in the resurrection of Jesus. The centrality of the chapter lies in the statement that the forgiveness of sins and justification come through Christ and are received by faith, not by works of the law. At the same time, the text preserves the order of testimony: first to the Jews, then to the Gentiles. The reaction of the Gentiles shows that salvation is also the work of God's grace, for they rejoice and glorify the Lord by hearing the word.

scholarViews.insight: Teaching about the Lord includes a miraculous demonstration of divine power, and the miracle confirms the authority of the message preached in Cyprus.
The church of Antioch receives the sending of Barnabas and Saul by divine direction, with laying on hands, fasting and prayer, showing a conscious and reverent missionary vocation.
Paul begins his speech by reminding the God of our fathers and the liberation of Egypt, to show the continuity between the history of Israel and the work of Christ.

questions: What does the chapter teach about how the church should discern calls and send workers?
Why does Paul begin his preaching by recounting the story of Israel before speaking directly of Jesus?
How does the joy of the disciples in the midst of persecution confront the idea that suffering always indicates the absence of God's blessing?
study.practice: Today, the church and believers can imitate Antioch: seek the will of God with prayer and fasting, support with discernment who is sent, and maintain faithfulness to the gospel even when there is resistance. It is also important to learn from Paul to explain Christ from the Scriptures, showing that the Christian faith is not an inadminus to the Bible, but to fulfill the promise of God. In personal practice, the chapter calls the reader to respond to the word in faith, not with envy or hardening, and to seek spiritual joy that does not depend on circumstances.
